subject: physics

items.q: Some very heavy nuclides, such as californium-252, can undergo spontaneous fission, whereas uranium-235 in a reactor undergoes neutron-induced fission. Which statement about spontaneous fission is correct?
items.correct: Energy is released when the nucleus splits into two fragments of comparable mass.
items.misconception: Energy is released as kinetic energy of an α particle that breaks off the nucleus.
items.why: Both processes are described as a heavy nucleus 'breaking up' and both are spontaneous, and fission is often introduced straight after α decay. Everyday 'splitting' does not suggest that the two pieces must be of similar size. Fission gives two fragments of comparable mass, for example barium and krypton from uranium, together with two or three neutrons. α decay removes only two protons and two neutrons: uranium-238 becomes thorium-234, not two medium-sized nuclei.
items.specStatementText: that energy is released in spontaneous and neutron-induced fission
items.random_wrong: Energy is released only once the material is hot enough for its nuclei to shake apart.

items.q: In one neutron-induced fission of uranium-235, ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3¹₀n. The atomic masses are 235.043928 u for uranium-235, 140.914403 u for barium-141 and 91.926173 u for krypton-92, and the mass of a neutron is 1.008665 u (the electron masses cancel). Take 1 u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 931.5 MeV c⁻², 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. How much energy is released in this fission?
items.why:
The neutron is described as a 'trigger' and the released neutrons as the means of continuing the chain, rather like a catalyst in chemistry, whose amount is not counted in the reaction. Students attend to the two large fragments. Write the mass of every particle on each side: Δm = (m_U + m_n) − (m_Ba + m_Kr + 3m_n). Leaving out the neutrons changes Δm by two neutron masses, about 2.0 u, more than ten times the true mass difference.

Working: Mass of reactants = 235.043928 u + 1.008665 u = 236.052593 u. Mass of products = 140.914403 u + 91.926173 u + 3(1.008665 u) = 235.866571 u. Δm = 236.052593 u − 235.866571 u = 0.186022 u = 0.186022 × 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 3.090 × 10⁻²⁸ kg. E = Δmc² = 3.090 × 10⁻²⁸ kg × (3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)² = 2.78 × 10⁻¹¹ J ≈ 2.8 × 10⁻¹¹ J. Check in MeV: 0.186022 u × 931.5 MeV u⁻¹ = 173.3 MeV = 173.3 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J = 2.77 × 10⁻¹¹ J ≈ 2.8 × 10⁻¹¹ J.
items.specStatementText: that energy is released in spontaneous and neutron-induced fission

items.q: In the fission ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴⁰₅₄Xe + ⁹⁴₃₈Sr + 2¹₀n, the binding energies per nucleon are 7.59 MeV for uranium-235, 8.29 MeV for xenon-140 and 8.59 MeV for strontium-94. A free neutron has no binding energy. Take 1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J. How much energy is released in this fission?
items.why:
The binding energy curve plots binding energy per nucleon, and fission is explained as a move 'up the curve', so the per-nucleon values are treated as if they were the energies of the nuclei. Energy released = Σ(A × E_b/A) for the products − Σ(A × E_b/A) for the reactants. The per-nucleon difference of about 0.9 MeV applies to each of the roughly 236 nucleons, giving about 200 MeV.

Working: Total binding energy = A × (binding energy per nucleon). Reactants: ²³⁵U: 235 × 7.59 MeV = 1783.65 MeV; neutron 0. Products: ¹⁴⁰Xe: 140 × 8.29 MeV = 1160.60 MeV; ⁹⁴Sr: 94 × 8.59 MeV = 807.46 MeV; total 1968.06 MeV; neutrons 0. Energy released = 1968.06 MeV − 1783.65 MeV = 184.41 MeV = 184.41 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J = 2.95 × 10⁻¹¹ J.
items.specStatementText: that energy is released in spontaneous and neutron-induced fission

Energy released = 1968.06 MeV − 1783.65 MeV = 184.41 MeV = 184.41 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J = 2.95 × 10⁻¹¹ J.

items.q: A chain reaction of uranium-235 fission in a reactor core is proceeding at a steady rate. Which condition is being met?
items.correct: On average, exactly one of the neutrons from each fission causes a further fission.
items.misconception: Each fission releases exactly one neutron, which goes on to cause a further fission.
items.why: Textbook diagrams of a chain reaction show each of the two or three neutrons from a fission hitting another nucleus, a branching tree with no neutrons lost. Count only the neutrons that cause fission. With 2.5 neutrons released per fission, 0.7 escaping and 0.8 absorbed, just 1.0 per fission causes another fission, and the rate stays constant.
items.specStatementText: the role of chain reactions in nuclear fission reactions
items.random_wrong: The fission fragments split again in turn, each one releasing further neutrons.

items.q: In a reactor core, each fission of uranium-235 releases 2.5 neutrons on average. Of these, on average 0.7 escape from the core and 0.8 are absorbed by the control rods and other materials without causing fission. What happens to the rate of fission?
items.correct: It stays constant: on average one neutron per fission causes a fission.
items.misconception: It decreases: control rods absorb neutrons and so shut the reaction down.
items.why:
Control rods are often introduced in the context of shutting down a reactor or an emergency, so their continuous role in holding the reaction steady is missed. Whether the rate rises, stays steady or falls depends on the number of neutrons per fission that cause a further fission, after all losses, including absorption by the rods. At constant power the rods absorb neutrons all the time, and that number is exactly one.

Working: Neutrons per fission that go on to cause a further fission = 2.5 − 0.7 − 0.8 = 1.0. Each generation therefore has the same number of fissions as the one before, so the rate of fission stays constant (the reactor is critical).
items.specStatementText: the role of chain reactions in nuclear fission reactions
items.random_wrong: It increases: each fission releases more neutrons than the one it absorbed.
items.working: Neutrons per fission that go on to cause a further fission = 2.5 − 0.7 − 0.8 = 1.0. Each generation therefore has the same number of fissions as the one before, so the rate of fission stays constant (the reactor is critical).

items.q: A sphere of pure uranium-235 has a mass slightly below the critical mass: a chain reaction started in it dies away. Which change, keeping the same mass of uranium-235, could allow it to sustain a chain reaction?
items.correct: Surround the sphere with a material that reflects escaping neutrons back into it
items.misconception: Place a strong neutron source beside the sphere so more fissions start
items.why: Students think of a fire, which keeps going if enough is lit at once, and a neutron source is described as 'starting' a reactor, so the number of starting neutrons seems to decide whether the reaction continues. A chain reaction is self-sustaining only if the number of fissions per generation is multiplied by at least one. That depends on the material, its mass, shape and surroundings, not on the number of neutrons supplied from outside.
items.specStatementText: the role of chain reactions in nuclear fission reactions
items.random_wrong: Heat the sphere strongly, so that its nuclei vibrate hard enough to split

items.q: In a gas-cooled reactor, the uranium fuel rods sit in channels through a large block of graphite, which is the moderator. Carbon dioxide gas carries thermal energy from the core. What is the role of the graphite?
items.correct: It slows fast neutrons by collisions, as slow neutrons are more likely to cause fission.
items.misconception: It absorbs surplus neutrons from the fuel, so that the rate of fission is kept under control.
items.why: In everyday language 'moderate' means to restrain or keep under control, so the moderator is taken to control the reaction, the job of the control rods. A moderator must absorb few neutrons, otherwise the chain reaction could not continue; its job is to slow them to thermal speeds. Neutron absorbers such as boron and cadmium are used in the control rods.
items.specStatementText: the role of control rods, moderators, heat exchangers and shielding in a nuclear power plant
items.random_wrong: It speeds up the neutrons so that they hit uranium nuclei hard enough to split them.

items.q: Pushing the control rods further into a reactor core reduces its power output. Why?
items.correct: They absorb neutrons, so fewer neutrons are left to cause fission.
items.misconception: They slow neutrons down, so the neutrons are less able to split nuclei.
items.why: Fission is drawn as a neutron 'smashing into' a nucleus, and in mechanics a harder impact breaks things more easily, so more kinetic energy seems to mean a greater chance of splitting. Neutron-induced fission starts with the absorption of the neutron, not with the impact. A slow neutron spends longer near a nucleus and is much more likely to be absorbed; the energy released comes from the mass difference, not from the neutron's kinetic energy.
items.specStatementText: the role of control rods, moderators, heat exchangers and shielding in a nuclear power plant
items.random_wrong: They absorb thermal energy, cooling the fuel so that fewer nuclei split.

items.q: In a pressurized water reactor, water pumped through the core (the primary coolant) becomes radioactive, but the water turned into steam to drive the turbine does not. What makes this possible?
items.correct: The circuits are separate: energy is conducted through heat-exchanger tube walls to water that does not enter the core.
items.misconception: The primary water mixes with cooler secondary water in the heat exchanger, which dilutes it until it is no longer radioactive.
items.why: Everyday mixing of hot and cold water is the most familiar way of warming water, and students believe that dilution makes a radioactive substance harmless because it makes a chemical solution weaker. Thermal energy can pass through a solid wall by conduction without any matter crossing it. Keeping the circuits separate means the radioactive nuclides in the primary coolant never reach the turbine; diluting radioactive material would spread it, not remove it.
items.specStatementText: the role of control rods, moderators, heat exchangers and shielding in a nuclear power plant
items.random_wrong: Boiling the water into steam in the heat exchanger destroys the radioactivity the water picked up in the core.

items.q: A reactor core is surrounded by thick layers of steel and concrete. What is the main purpose of these layers?
items.correct: To absorb the neutrons and γ radiation leaving the core, protecting people nearby
items.misconception: To stop α particles from the fuel, the most ionizing and most harmful radiation
items.why: Students learn that α particles are the most ionizing and most harmful when inside the body, and apply this to every situation without considering whether the radiation can reach a person. How dangerous a radiation is depends on whether it reaches the body as well as on how ionizing it is. α particles from the fuel cannot leave it; neutrons and γ rays penetrate far and need thick steel and concrete to absorb them.
items.specStatementText: the role of control rods, moderators, heat exchangers and shielding in a nuclear power plant
items.random_wrong: To contain the explosion if the chain reaction runs out of control, as in a bomb

items.q: A fission of uranium-235 produces barium-141 (¹⁴¹₅₆Ba) and krypton-92 (⁹²₃₆Kr). The heaviest stable isotopes of these elements are barium-138 (¹³⁸₅₆Ba) and krypton-86 (⁸⁶₃₆Kr). Which decay are barium-141 and krypton-92 expected to undergo?
items.correct: β⁻ decay, which turns a surplus neutron into a proton
items.misconception: β⁺ decay, which converts a surplus neutron into a proton
items.why:
The signs are easily reversed: students connect the '+' with the proton being produced, or remember that one β decay turns a neutron into a proton without remembering which. Use conservation of charge. β⁻ decay emits a negative electron, so the nucleus gains positive charge: a neutron becomes a proton. β⁺ decay emits a positive positron, so the nucleus loses positive charge: a proton becomes a neutron.

Working: Barium-141 has N = 141 − 56 = 85 neutrons; stable barium has at most 138 − 56 = 82. Krypton-92 has N = 92 − 36 = 56; stable krypton has at most 86 − 36 = 50. Both fragments have surplus neutrons, so they undergo β⁻ decay, in which a neutron changes into a proton (Z increases by 1, N decreases by 1).
items.specStatementText: the properties of the products of nuclear fission and their management.
items.random_wrong: α decay, which carries the surplus neutrons away
items.working: Barium-141 has N = 141 − 56 = 85 neutrons; stable barium has at most 138 − 56 = 82. Krypton-92 has N = 92 − 36 = 56; stable krypton has at most 86 − 36 = 50. Both fragments have surplus neutrons, so they undergo β⁻ decay, in which a neutron changes into a proton (Z increases by 1, N decreases by 1).

items.q: Spent fuel rods taken out of a reactor are stored for several years under a few metres of water in a pool. No chain reaction takes place in the pool, yet the pool water has to be cooled continuously. Why does the water need cooling?
items.correct: The radioactive fission products keep decaying, and their decay energy heats the rods.
items.misconception: The rods still hold the thermal energy they gained in the core, which leaks out only slowly.
items.why: Everyday hot objects cool steadily once removed from their heat source, so the fuel is pictured as a stored-up hot object rather than a continuing source of energy. A fuel rod simply cooling down would lose its thermal energy in hours in cold water. Pools must be cooled for years because the fission products continue to release energy as they decay, at a rate that falls as the short-lived products decay away.
items.specStatementText: the properties of the products of nuclear fission and their management.
items.random_wrong: Keeping the rods cold slows down the decay of their fission products, making them safer.

items.q: High-level waste from a reactor contains caesium-137, a fission product with a half-life of 30 years. The waste is kept in a store for 90 years. What percentage of the initial caesium-137 activity remains at the end of this time?
items.why:
Both numbers describe 'how much decay has happened', and students divide by the number of half-lives, as they would divide a quantity shared equally. Halve the activity once for each half-life: after 1, 2 and 3 half-lives, 50%, 25% and 12.5% remain.

Working: Number of half-lives = 90 years ÷ 30 years = 3. Fraction of the activity remaining = (½)³ = ⅛ = 0.125, so 12.5% remains.
items.specStatementText: the properties of the products of nuclear fission and their management.
items.working: Number of half-lives = 90 years ÷ 30 years = 3. Fraction of the activity remaining = (½)³ = ⅛ = 0.125, so 12.5% remains.

items.q: Spent fuel contains caesium-137 (half-life 30 years), strontium-90 (half-life 29 years) and technetium-99 (half-life 2.1 × 10⁵ years), produced in similar numbers by fission. Which conclusion about the long-term storage of this waste is correct?
items.correct: It stays radioactive for far longer than 300 years, as the technetium-99 barely decays in that time.
items.misconception: After about 60 years, two of their half-lives, the caesium-137 and strontium-90 in it have completely decayed.
items.why:
In everyday language 'half-time' or 'half-way' refers to half of a fixed total duration, and linear thinking suggests that if half goes in one half-life the other half goes in the next. The number of undecayed nuclei, and hence the activity, falls by a factor of 2 in every half-life: ½, ¼, ⅛, … After two half-lives a quarter remains.

Working: After 300 years (about 10 half-lives) the caesium-137 and strontium-90 activities have fallen to about (½)¹⁰ ≈ 1/1000 of their initial values. In 300 years technetium-99 completes only 300/(2.1 × 10⁵) ≈ 0.0014 of a half-life, so almost all of it remains. For similar numbers of nuclei, far fewer technetium-99 nuclei decay each second than caesium-137 nuclei, so its activity is much smaller at first, but it persists for hundreds of thousands of years.
items.specStatementText: the properties of the products of nuclear fission and their management.
items.random_wrong: Most of its activity at first comes from technetium-99, as it has by far the longest half-life of the three.
items.working: After 300 years (about 10 half-lives) the caesium-137 and strontium-90 activities have fallen to about (½)¹⁰ ≈ 1/1000 of their initial values. In 300 years technetium-99 completes only 300/(2.1 × 10⁵) ≈ 0.0014 of a half-life, so almost all of it remains. For similar numbers of nuclei, far fewer technetium-99 nuclei decay each second than caesium-137 nuclei, so its activity is much smaller at first, but it persists for hundreds of thousands of years.

items.q: Does a nucleus need to be hot to undergo fission, and does the heat released make more nuclei split?
items.correct: No. Spontaneous fission is random with a fixed probability per unit time, unaffected by temperature, and neutron-induced fission is caused by the absorption of a neutron. The thermal energy released in the fuel does not make further nuclei split; neutrons do.
items.misconception: Nuclei split when the fuel is hot enough: fission is driven by temperature, the heat released by one fission makes further nuclei split, and the fission rate can be controlled by heating or cooling the fuel.
items.why: Fission and fusion are learned together and their names are easily confused; fusion does need very high temperatures. Reactors are described as 'hot' and chemical fires spread because the heat released ignites more fuel, so a nuclear chain reaction is pictured in the same way. Fission needs no high temperature. A chain reaction is carried from one fission to the next by neutrons, and its rate is set by how many neutrons from each fission go on to cause another fission. The thermal energy of the fuel is far too small to split a nucleus.
items.specStatementText: that energy is released in spontaneous and neutron-induced fission
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where does the energy released in neutron-induced fission come from?
items.correct: From the decrease in rest mass: the products have less total mass than the reactants, and E = Δmc². The absorbed neutron need bring almost no kinetic energy; spontaneous fission, with no neutron at all, also releases energy.
items.misconception: The energy released in fission is supplied by the neutron that is absorbed, so a nucleus that splits without absorbing a neutron releases no energy.
items.why: Neutron-induced fission is shown as a neutron striking a nucleus, and from mechanics students expect the energy of a break-up to come from the impact. The neutron is the only visible 'input' in the equation. The kinetic energy of a thermal neutron is about 0.025 eV, while a fission releases about 200 MeV. The energy comes from the increase in binding energy (decrease in rest mass) when a heavy nucleus becomes two medium-mass nuclei; this is the same whether the fission is spontaneous or neutron-induced.
items.specStatementText: that energy is released in spontaneous and neutron-induced fission
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is the energy equivalent of a mass found?
items.correct: By multiplying the mass by the square of the speed of light: E = Δmc², with c² = 9.00 × 10¹⁶ m² s⁻² when the mass is in kg.
items.misconception: The energy equivalent of a mass is found by multiplying the mass by the speed of light, c.
items.why: The equation is quoted so often as 'E equals m c squared' that the square is dropped in calculation, and equations such as p = mv have a mass multiplied by a single speed. Check the units: kg × m s⁻¹ is kg m s⁻¹, a momentum, whereas kg × m² s⁻² is J. The energy equivalent needs c².
items.specStatementText: that energy is released in spontaneous and neutron-induced fission
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is an energy in MeV converted to joules?
items.misconception: An energy in MeV is converted to joules by multiplying by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹, as for an energy in electronvolts; the prefix 'mega' can be ignored.
items.why: The conversion factor 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ is memorized for the electronvolt, and the unit prefix is overlooked when the number in MeV is multiplied by it. Convert the prefix as well: an energy of 173 MeV is 173 × 10⁶ eV = 1.73 × 10⁸ eV, which is 1.73 × 10⁸ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 2.77 × 10⁻¹¹ J.
items.specStatementText: that energy is released in spontaneous and neutron-induced fission
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the energy released in fission the binding energy of the uranium nucleus?
items.correct: No. The binding energy of uranium-235 is the energy that would have to be supplied to separate it into free nucleons. The energy released in fission is the increase in total binding energy when uranium becomes more tightly bound fragments.
items.misconception: Binding energy is energy stored in the uranium nucleus, and when the nucleus splits this stored binding energy is released.
items.why: In chemistry, energy is said to be 'stored in bonds' and released when they break, and nuclear energy is described as energy 'locked up' in the nucleus. 'Binding energy' sounds like an amount the nucleus contains. Splitting the uranium nucleus completely into nucleons would need its whole binding energy, about 1780 MeV. Fission releases energy only because the fragments have a greater total binding energy than the uranium: about 200 MeV per fission.
items.specStatementText: that energy is released in spontaneous and neutron-induced fission
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the energy released in fission equal to the binding energy of the products?
items.correct: No. The energy released is the binding energy of the products minus the binding energy of the reactants. The uranium nucleus was already bound, so only the increase is released.
items.misconception: The energy released in fission is the total binding energy of the nuclei formed, because binding energy is released when those nuclei form.
items.why: Binding energy is correctly taught as the energy released when a nucleus forms from separate nucleons, and students apply this to the fragments without noticing that their nucleons were not free beforehand. The nucleons of the fragments came from a uranium nucleus that was already bound by about 7.6 MeV per nucleon. Subtract the reactants' total binding energy from the products' total binding energy.
items.specStatementText: that energy is released in spontaneous and neutron-induced fission
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do the fission fragments split again to continue a chain reaction?
items.correct: No. The fragments, such as barium-141 and krypton-92, are medium-mass nuclei that do not undergo fission; they decay by β⁻ emission. The chain is carried by the neutrons released in each fission.
items.misconception: The fragments produced by a fission split again, and this repeated splitting of smaller and smaller pieces is the chain reaction.
items.why: 'Chain reaction' suggests pieces breaking into smaller pieces, as in a cascade, and diagrams draw the fragments next to the new fissions, so the fragments seem to be what goes on to split. Medium-mass fragments such as barium-141 and krypton-92 are not fissile: absorbing a neutron does not make them split, and any energy gained from splitting them would be far smaller than from splitting uranium. Being neutron-rich, they decay by β⁻ emission instead. The neutrons from each fission, not the fragments, are absorbed by further uranium-235 nuclei.
items.specStatementText: the role of chain reactions in nuclear fission reactions
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does breaking fuel into small pieces increase the fission rate, as a larger surface area speeds up a chemical reaction?
items.correct: No. Breaking the fuel into small pieces increases the surface area compared with the volume, so a larger fraction of neutrons escapes before causing fission and the chain reaction dies away more quickly.
items.misconception: Cutting the fuel into smaller pieces exposes more of its surface, so more nuclei are available to neutrons and fission is more likely, as a powder reacts faster than a lump.
items.why: In chemistry, increasing surface area increases the rate of reaction, and students transfer this rule to nuclear fuel, where the neutrons come from inside the fuel rather than from outside it. The neutrons that sustain the chain are produced inside the fuel. The more surface there is compared with volume, the more of them escape. This is why there is a critical mass, and why a large lump can be critical when the same mass in small pieces is not.
items.specStatementText: the role of chain reactions in nuclear fission reactions
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the moderator there to keep the reactor core cool?
items.correct: No. The moderator slows neutrons down; the coolant carries thermal energy from the core. In a graphite-moderated, gas-cooled reactor these are different materials.
items.misconception: The moderator 'moderates' the temperature of the core: its role is to keep the fuel from overheating by absorbing thermal energy.
items.why: The word 'moderate' suggests keeping something at a moderate level, and temperature is the most familiar quantity to keep moderate. In water-cooled reactors the same water acts as both coolant and moderator, which blurs the two roles. The moderator is defined by what it does to neutrons: it slows them to thermal energies through collisions with light nuclei. Removing thermal energy is the job of the coolant, which delivers it to the heat exchanger.

items.q: Does heating or cooling a radioactive material change its radioactivity?
items.correct: No. The rate of radioactive decay is not affected by temperature, pressure or chemical change. Heating, boiling or cooling a sample leaves its half-life and activity unchanged.
items.misconception: Radioactivity can be changed by temperature: heating or boiling a radioactive material destroys its radioactivity, and cooling it slows the decay and makes it safer.
items.why: Most processes students know, such as chemical reactions, evaporation and decay of food, go faster when hot and slower when cold, so radioactive decay is assumed to behave in the same way. Radioactive decay is a change in the nucleus and is random with a fixed probability per unit time. Temperature changes the motion of atoms and molecules but has no measurable effect on decay rates, so spent fuel is cooled to remove its decay heat, not to slow its decay.
items.specStatementText: the properties of the products of nuclear fission and their management.

items.q: Does exposure to radiation make a material radioactive?
items.correct: Not in general. Exposure to α, β or γ radiation does not make a material radioactive. Water or steel becomes radioactive only if radioactive material gets into it or if its nuclei are changed, for example by absorbing neutrons in the core.
items.misconception: Anything exposed to radiation becomes radioactive itself, so water or metal near radioactive material becomes radioactive.
items.why: Radiation and radioactive contamination are both called 'radiation' in everyday speech, and objects near a source are described as 'exposed', suggesting that some of the radioactivity passes into them. Distinguish irradiation from contamination. γ photons absorbed by water deposit energy but leave the water's nuclei unchanged. The secondary water in a reactor stays non-radioactive because it never passes through the core and never mixes with the primary coolant.

items.q: Can a nuclear reactor explode like a nuclear bomb?
items.correct: No. Power-reactor fuel contains only a few per cent of uranium-235, or less, and is spread through a moderator, so it cannot produce the rapid, uncontrolled chain reaction of a bomb. Serious reactor accidents involve overheating, steam or chemical explosions and the release of radioactive material.
items.misconception: A reactor whose chain reaction ran out of control would explode like a nuclear bomb, and the thick shielding is there to contain such an explosion.
items.why: Reactors and nuclear weapons both use fission chain reactions and are often discussed together, and the word 'nuclear' is associated with explosions. The shielding around the core is there to absorb neutrons and γ radiation during normal operation. A nuclear explosion needs nearly pure fissile material assembled into a supercritical mass extremely quickly, which a reactor cannot do.
items.specStatementText: the role of control rods, moderators, heat exchangers and shielding in a nuclear power plant
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the shielding around a reactor a thermal insulator to keep energy in the core?
items.correct: No. The shielding absorbs neutrons and γ radiation to protect people. Thermal energy is removed from the core by the coolant and transferred to the heat exchanger.
items.misconception: The thick layers around the core are there to keep thermal energy in, like insulation, so that less of the energy released is wasted to the surroundings.
items.why: Insulation around hot equipment is familiar from domestic heating, and a thick wall around the hottest part of a power station seems to be there to keep the heat in. The purpose of shielding is protection from radiation. The thermal energy is carried away by the coolant; the shielding's thickness is set by how far neutrons and γ rays penetrate, not by heat loss.
items.specStatementText: the role of control rods, moderators, heat exchangers and shielding in a nuclear power plant

items.q: Are the products of fission stable, harmless nuclei?
items.correct: No. Fission fragments are neutron-rich and radioactive, mostly β⁻ and γ emitters, with half-lives from fractions of a second to hundreds of thousands of years. They make spent fuel highly radioactive.
items.misconception: Fission splits a large, unstable nucleus into smaller, stable nuclei, such as ordinary barium and krypton, so the products are not radioactive and can at most give out a little energy as γ rays.
items.why: Smaller nuclei are associated with stability, and the products are named after familiar elements. Students do not compare the neutron number of a fragment with that of the stable isotopes of the same element. A heavy nucleus has many more neutrons than protons. The fragments keep this high neutron-to-proton ratio, so they have far more neutrons than the stable isotopes of their elements: barium-141 has 85 neutrons, but the heaviest stable barium isotope, barium-138, has 82.

items.q: Does α decay get rid of surplus neutrons?
items.correct: No. An α particle carries away two protons and two neutrons, so α decay hardly changes the ratio of neutrons to protons. Neutron-rich fragments decay by β⁻ emission.
items.misconception: α decay is how a nucleus gets rid of surplus neutrons, since the α particle carries neutrons away.
items.why: Students know that α particles contain neutrons and that α decay makes a nucleus smaller, and assume that making it smaller removes the excess. An α particle removes equal numbers of protons and neutrons. For a neutron-rich medium-mass fragment, this would increase the neutron-to-proton ratio slightly rather than reduce it. β⁻ decay changes a neutron into a proton and brings the nucleus closer to stability.

items.q: How many half-lives are there in a sequence of times 0, T, 2T, 3T?
items.correct: Three. The number of half-lives is the number of intervals between the listed times, not the number of times listed.
items.misconception: The number of half-lives is the number of values in the sequence, including the starting value, so the times 0, 30, 60 and 90 years represent four half-lives.
items.why: Students list the times or halving values and count them, a 'fencepost' error: four posts mark only three gaps. Count the intervals, or divide the elapsed time by the half-life: 90 years ÷ 30 years = 3 half-lives, so the activity is halved three times.

items.q: Do nuclides with long half-lives have the greatest activity?
items.correct: No. For similar numbers of nuclei, a longer half-life means that fewer of the nuclei decay each second, and so a smaller activity. Long-lived products matter for storage because their activity persists, not because it is high.
items.misconception: Nuclides with long half-lives are the most radioactive, so for similar numbers of nuclei a longer half-life gives a greater activity.
items.why: 'Long-lasting' is heard as 'powerful', and long-lived waste is rightly described as a long-term hazard, which students turn into 'highly radioactive'. Activity is the number of decays per second. In 30 years half of a sample of caesium-137 decays, but almost none of a sample of technetium-99 does, so equal numbers of nuclei give a far greater activity for caesium-137.

items.q: Does absorbing radiation reduce the activity of radioactive waste?
items.correct: No. Shielding or burial absorbs the radiation emitted, protecting people, but the activity of the waste, the number of nuclei decaying per second, is unchanged; it falls only as the nuclei decay.
items.misconception: Surrounding radioactive waste with material that absorbs its radiation, such as rock, water or concrete, reduces the activity of the waste.
items.why: 'Radiation' and 'radioactivity' are used interchangeably in everyday speech, so stopping the radiation is taken to reduce the radioactivity itself. Activity is the number of nuclei decaying per second; it depends only on how many undecayed nuclei there are and on their half-lives. A shield reduces how much radiation reaches people, not how many nuclei decay; the waste stays active as long as its half-lives dictate.

items.q: After three half-lives, is 87.5% of the activity left?
items.correct: No. After three half-lives ⅛ (12.5%) of the undecayed nuclei, and so of the activity, remains; ⅞ (87.5%) of the nuclei have decayed.
items.misconception: The fraction of a sample that has decayed and the fraction that remains are the same quantity, so after three half-lives the answer is 1 − ⅛ = 87.5% of the activity.
items.why: Questions ask sometimes for the fraction decayed and sometimes for the fraction remaining, and both are found from the same halving sequence. Students calculate one and report it as the other. Decide first which quantity is asked for. The activity is proportional to the number of nuclei that have NOT yet decayed: (½)ⁿ of the initial value after n half-lives. The fraction decayed is 1 − (½)ⁿ.
